Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the sources of the Fourth Gospel.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Fourth Gospel is anonymous, and the question of its sources is much discussed. To examine them critically means to set out the possible sources and to weigh the strength of the evidence for each one. The Gospel probably draws on several sources: the testimony of an eyewitness, earlier Christian tradition, the Old Testament and the Jewish and Greek thought of its day.

**1. Eyewitness testimony.** The Gospel speaks of the beloved disciple as the one who bears witness to what is written (John 21:24; see also 19:35). Church tradition from the late second century, for example Irenaeus, identifies him with John the son of Zebedee. Details such as the names of people and places, the time of day (for example John 4:6) and the topography of Jerusalem suggest an informed source. But the Gospel itself does not name the disciple, and the identification is debated: some scholars propose John the Elder, or a disciple who was not one of the Twelve, or a Johannine community of which the beloved disciple was the founder.

**2. The Synoptic Gospels.** Many details are shared with Mark and Luke, such as the feeding of the five thousand, the walking on the water, the anointing, the Last Supper and the Passion narrative. Some scholars think John knew one or more of the Synoptic Gospels; others hold that he used independent traditions. The great differences in structure, in the chronology of the ministry and in the content of the teaching speak against simple copying.

**3. A source of signs.** Some scholars argue that the evangelist used a collection of miracle stories, numbered in John 2:11 and 4:54, as a "signs source". This is a scholarly theory and is not certain.

**4. The Old Testament and Jewish thought.** The Gospel begins with an echo of Genesis 1 ("In the beginning"). It uses images from Moses and the manna (John 6), the serpent in the wilderness (John 3:14), the Passover lamb (John 1:29, 19:36), and the feasts of the Jewish year. The Wisdom tradition of the Old Testament lies behind the Prologue (John 1:1-18). Ideas of light and darkness are also found in the writings of the Qumran community, which shows a Jewish background.

**5. Greek influence.** The term *Logos* (Word) was used by Greek philosophers and by the Jewish thinker Philo, so some scholars see Hellenistic influence. Others argue that the Jewish idea of the Word of God and of Wisdom is a sufficient source.

**6. The evangelist's own reflection.** The Gospel states that the Spirit would remind the disciples of what Jesus had said (John 14:26), so the long discourses may be the fruit of decades of preaching and reflection in the church.

**Conclusion.** The evidence suggests that the Fourth Gospel rests on a mixture of eyewitness memory, Christian tradition, Scripture and the thought-world of the evangelist's community. It is not possible to settle the question with certainty, and the exact relationship to the Synoptics and to the beloved disciple remains open.
